narrative.h2: Folk videos earn their quiet through restraint

sections.heading: What folk looks like
sections.body: Folk visuals trade spectacle for intimacy. The camera tends to sit still or drift slowly — handheld but composed, not shaky. Natural light does most of the work: a kitchen window at golden hour, a porch at dusk, a forest clearing under overcast sky. Wardrobe is lived-in wool and denim, never costume. The artist usually appears mid-task — pouring coffee, tuning a guitar, walking — rather than performing directly to lens.

sections.heading: Reference points that actually work
sections.body: Bon Iver's Holocene set the template: a small figure inside an enormous landscape, no narrative arc required. Phoebe Bridgers' Kyoto leans into the same restraint but adds dry humor. Fleet Foxes' Helplessness Blues and the long arc of Sufjan Stevens videos sit nearby. The shared grammar: 35mm grain or its digital cousin, long lenses for distance, hands and faces in close-up, weather as a co-star. Almost never wide-angle, almost never cool blue.

sections.heading: Prompting tip for Tunee
sections.body: Resist adjectives that push toward 'cinematic'. Instead, anchor each scene in a small physical detail: 'fingers on the third fret', 'breath visible in November air', 'rain on a kitchen window'. Tunee responds well to time-of-day cues — 'first light', 'last hour before sunset' — because they constrain palette automatically. Keep edits long and let one moment finish before the next begins. Folk is the genre where cutting too fast kills the song.
